query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a direct energy deposition (DED) process with a rapid cooling rate (≥10^4 K/s) followed by a short annealing step just below the recrystallization temperature will produce an ultra-fine grained Ti–Ni primary HEA, resulting in a 15–25% increase in elevated-temperature yield strength relative to conventionally cooled alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy (approximately 35 at.% Ti and 35 at.% Ni with minor alloying additions) produced via conventional DED that typically exhibits a coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the DED process parameters to achieve a high cooling rate (≥10^4 K/s) during deposition and apply a subsequent brief annealing at ~950 °C (just below the recrystallization threshold) for 15 minutes.
generation.conditions: DED processed under controlled laser power and scan speed to ensure the required cooling rate; annealing conducted under an inert atmosphere with a temperature window of 925–975 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultra-fine grain structure with reduced average grain size, leading to enhanced grain boundary strengthening as per the Hall–Petch relationship.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement increases yield strength by introducing a higher density of grain boundaries that impede dislocation motion, particularly under elevated temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Elevated-temperature (e.g., 800 °C) yield strength increases by approximately 15–25% compared to conventionally processed, coarser-grained samples.
generation.baseline: A Ti–Ni primary HEA fabricated by standard DED parameters leading to a coarser microstructure without the additional rapid cooling and annealing step.
generation.boundary: Effective when the cooling rate is maintained above 10^4 K/s and the short annealing does not trigger significant grain growth; applicable for Ti and Ni concentrations typical of the primary phase (30–35 at%).
generation.uncertainty: The robustness of grain size retention at long-term elevated temperatures; sensitivity of the microstructure to slight changes in DED parameters or annealing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce samples using both the modified rapid-cooling DED process with annealing and conventional DED processing. Characterize grain size using EBSD, and perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (at 800 °C) to measure yield strength.
measurements: Fractography to ensure no deleterious phases formed
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultra-fine grained samples do not show at least a 15% improvement in yield strength at 800 °C compared to the controls, or if the grain size remains similar between samples, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, a Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEA was deposited using DED. The phase diagram and phase fraction of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were analyzed for deposition on Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. For the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, powders of each element were mixed to prepare a mixed Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al powder and deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates. The microstructure and hardness of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were measured. In addition, HAZ and thermal shielding analyses were performed on the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. The primary findings of this study are as follows: SEM images and EBSD analysis were used to investigate the microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. Phase analysis predicted that the BCC B2 phase was 62.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 21.6%, and C14 Laves phase was 16.2%. However, the σ phase was 64.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 28.2%, and the Ti2Ni phase was 7.6% in the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.The microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al consisted of a phase not predicted by the phase analysis but showed a microstructure similar to that of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al annealed after casting. In addition, the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al exhibited a fine grain size of 1–35 μm.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti High-Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA (with Ti and Al as key alloying constituents in a predominantly Ni-based FCC matrix)
papers.approach: Utilized additive manufacturing (DED) to produce an HEA designed to form a dual-phase microstructure (γ + γ′) via controlled Al + Ti additions.
papers.findings: A uniform distribution of ordered γ′ precipitates ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) was achieved in a Ni-rich FCC matrix, resulting in improved tensile strength and microhardness alongside thermal stability at ~800 °C.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via formation of a coherent, ordered γ′ phase that impedes dislocation motion.

papers.title: Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions.
papers.approach: Varied the Zr content in a Ti-based medium-entropy alloy to assess effects on grain size, yield strength, and ductility.
papers.findings: Increasing Zr content yielded modest increases in yield strength (3–8%) with trade-offs in ductility due to microstructural coarsening; an optimum composition (Zr7) was identified for further thermomechanical treatment.
papers.mechanism: A combination of substitutional solid solution strengthening and grain size effects; Zr’s larger atomic size induced lattice distortion and grain growth.

papers.title: The Microstructures, Mechanical Properties, and Deformation Mechanism of B2-Hardened NbTiAlZr-Based Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: NbTiAlZr-based refractory HEA (with Ti as a principal constituent alongside Nb, Al, and Zr)
papers.approach: Employed rapid solidification and compositional tuning to produce a B2-ordered matrix with antiphase boundaries (APBs), then analyzed phase evolution with varying Zr levels.
papers.findings: Confirmed formation of an ordered B2 phase whose lattice constant increases with greater Zr content; the presence of APBs and adjustable phase fractions correlated with improved yield strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening via lattice distortion and ordering effects (B2 phase) that interact with dislocations, although the direct contribution of APBs to yield strength is limited.

papers.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Non-equiatomic HEA designed for high nanoprecipitate volume fraction (primarily Ni-based matrix with high-content coherent Ni3Al-type precipitates)
papers.approach: Tailored alloy composition (increasing Ni/Al ratio) to trigger spinodal decomposition that forms a dual microstructure with a disordered FCC matrix and ordered L12 nanoprecipitates.
papers.findings: Achieved an ultrahigh tensile strength of ~1.9 GPa and ductility exceeding 9%, attributed to the high volume fraction (>50 vol%) of coherent precipitates that maintain low misfit with the matrix.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via coherent, ductile nanoprecipitates that both act as obstacles to dislocation motion and generate antiphase boundaries on slip planes.

papers.title: Influence of Titanium on Microstructure, Phase Formation and Wear Behaviour of AlCoCrFeNiTiₓ High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTiₓ HEA with variable titanium content
papers.approach: Investigated the effect of increasing titanium content on phase formation, microstructural heterogeneity, and wear behavior through controlled alloying.
papers.findings: At low Ti contents, a single ordered BCC phase was observed; with increased Ti, the microstructure became heterogeneous featuring dendritic structures and additional interdendritic (and possibly intermetallic) phases that influence hardness and wear resistance.
papers.mechanism: Titanium’s large atomic radius promotes solid solution strengthening but also leads to the precipitation of secondary intermetallic compounds if its concentration exceeds a threshold.

papers.title: Development of Precipitation-Strengthened Al₀.₈NbTiVM (M = Co, Ni) Light-Weight Refractory High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Al₀.₈NbTiV HEA alloy modified with minor Co or Ni additions
papers.approach: Designed a lightweight refractory HEA with a base of Al₀.₈NbTiV and introduced Co or Ni to stimulate the formation of fine sigma precipitates; compared as-cast and heat-treated conditions.
papers.findings: The introduction of Co or Ni resulted in homogeneous distribution of sigma precipitates, leading to an increase in yield strength (and superior specific yield strength at elevated temperatures) without severely compromising ductility.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced yield strength is attributed to a combination of solid solution strengthening (via the smaller atomic radii of Co and Ni) and precipitation strengthening from sigma phase formation within a BCC matrix.

papers.title: High-entropy alloy strengthened by in situ formation of entropy-stabilized nano-dispersoids.
papers.system: Al₀.₃CoCrFeMnNi HEA reinforced with 3 vol.% Y₂O₃
papers.approach: Reinforced a base HEA with a minor volume fraction of Y₂O₃ via spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders to induce the formation of nanoscale dispersoids.
papers.findings: The addition of Y₂O₃ increased the compressive yield strength from approximately 980 MPa to 1759 MPa, largely attributed to the dispersion strengthening provided by the entropy-stabilized nano-dispersoids combined with grain refinement.
papers.mechanism: Dispersion strengthening through nano-oxides that impede dislocation motion, supplemented by a grain size reduction effect.

papers.title: The Effect of Al and Ti Additions on Solid Solution Strengthening and Precipitation Hardening in CoNiFe Medium-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoNiFe-based medium-entropy alloy with minor Al and Ti additions
papers.approach: Explored the strengthening effects of adding 5 at.% Al and/or Ti to a CoNiFe base alloy, focusing on differences in lattice distortion and precipitation behavior.
papers.findings: While 5 at.% Al provided negligible solid solution strengthening, the addition of 5 at.% Ti significantly increased strength via both solid solution and pronounced precipitation hardening through formation of (CoNi)₃Ti or γ′ phases.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced strengthening is primarily a result of precipitation hardening, where Ti promotes the formation of coherent, intermetallic precipitates that effectively obstruct dislocation motion.

papers.title: Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys.
papers.approach: Investigated the role of each constituent via a subtraction method and compared alloys with different element combinations to study elevated-temperature performance.
papers.findings: Alloys containing higher-melting elements (e.g., Ti, Zr) showed reduced density and varying elevated-temperature strengths. The study highlighted trade-offs in adjusting elemental fractions to optimize strength, ductility, and density.
papers.mechanism: Elemental contributions affect solid solution and high-temperature strength through lattice distortion, melting point, and interaction effects; Ti influences both strength and density.

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al Refractory High-Entropy Alloys Using Direct Energy Deposition.
papers.system: Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al refractory HEA (with Ti and Ni as two of the major constituents)
papers.approach: Employed direct energy deposition (DED) to manufacture a refractory HEA and performed phase analysis, microstructural characterization, and hardness testing.
papers.findings: The deposited alloy exhibited a multiphase microstructure (including sigma, BCC phases, and Ti2Ni) with fine grain sizes (1–35 μm) and high microhardness (~900 HV). The local thermal cycles from DED produced a refined microstructure that may benefit high-temperature performance.
papers.mechanism: Rapid solidification induced by DED leads to fine grains and complex phase formation; specific phase assemblages (involving Ti and Ni) impart strength at elevated temperatures through both grain-boundary and precipitation strengthening.

established: Precipitation strengthening via the formation of coherent, ordered phases (e.g., γ′, sigma, L12 nanoprecipitates) is effective at enhancing yield strength and elevated-temperature stability in HEAs.
Solid solution strengthening due to lattice distortion, particularly when using elements with different atomic radii (e.g., Ti’s large radius), plays a key role in HEA performance.
Grain refinement, whether achieved through thermomechanical processing or rapid solidification (e.g., via DED), consistently improves high-temperature mechanical properties.
HEA compositional design benefits from deviations from strictly equiatomic ratios, enabling the formation of multiphase microstructures that can balance strength and ductility.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying additions to a Ni-based matrix (e.g., Al + Ti to generate γ + γ′ phases) using DED processing
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced thermal stability and strength (~800 °C) via precipitate formation, as evidenced by increased tensile strength and hardness.

approaches_tried.approach: Adjustment of minor alloying elements (e.g., Zr, Co, or Ni) to modify grain size and induce precipitation
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved yield strength and ductility in refractory and medium-entropy alloys, though with sensitivity to grain coarsening at high additive levels.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ formation of nano-dispersoids (e.g., Y₂O₃ addition) in a base HEA
approaches_tried.outcome: Significant increase in compressive yield strength (from ~980 to ~1759 MPa) due to dispersion strengthening and grain refinement.

mechanisms: Precipitation strengthening via coherent precipitates (γ′, sigma, L12 phases) that impede dislocation motion.
Solid solution strengthening induced by lattice distortion from size-mismatched alloying elements.
Grain boundary strengthening resulting from refined microstructures achieved by rapid solidification or thermomechanical processing.
Dispersion strengthening through the introduction of stable, nano-scale particles.
disagreements: The extent to which antiphase boundaries (APBs) in ordered structures (e.g., B2 phase) contribute to yield strength is debated, with some studies indicating a limited effect.

The balance between achieving high strength via precipitate formation and retaining ductility remains controversial, particularly with high titanium levels that may promote brittle intermetallic phases.
open_questions: How will a high-entropy alloy system with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (rather than as minor additions) behave with respect to phase stability and elevated-temperature mechanical properties?

What are the precise compositional ranges and processing conditions that favor the formation of beneficial coherent precipitates in a Ti–Ni primary system without triggering detrimental intermetallic embrittlement?
How can the interactions between major constituents (Ti and Ni) be tuned to maximize solid solution and precipitation strengthening simultaneously at elevated temperatures?
opportunities: Investigate a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy by intentionally designing the base composition to include both elements in high concentrations (within 5–35 at% each), then introducing a minor controlled addition (or heat treatment intervention) aimed at enhancing precipitation (e.g., forming coherent σ or γ′ phases).

Combine rapid solidification techniques (such as DED) with tailored thermomechanical processing to refine the grain structure and stimulate the in situ formation of nano-precipitates in a Ti–Ni dominant system.

Explore microalloying strategies (using elements with smaller atomic radii than Ti) to promote a desirable lattice distortion and coherency between phases, ensuring improved yield strength and thermal stability without loss of ductility.

Perform systematic experiments varying processing parameters and minor element additions to map out the phase evolution and mechanical response specifically in Ti- and Ni-primary HEAs, thereby filling the current gap in literature.

directions.direction: Heat treatment to induce coherent gamma′ precipitation
directions.assessment: Directly targets elevated‐temperature strength by forming fine, coherent precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti-like phases) in a Ti–Ni primary matrix. Evidence on γ+γ′ microstructures (PMC11396108) supports this approach and it is feasible with controlled annealing schedules.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical processing via rapid solidification (DED) for grain refinement
directions.assessment: Improving strength via fine-grained microstructures is a well-known mechanism; DED’s rapid cooling can yield fine grains. Prior studies (PMC9571103) demonstrate refined grain structures under rapid solidification. The intervention is directly linked to high‐temperature yield.

directions.direction: In situ formation of nano-dispersoids via oxide additions (Y2O3)
directions.assessment: Dispersion strengthening by nano-oxides is supported by literature (PMC6148222). Although less common in Ti–Ni primary HEAs, adapting it may impart additional dislocation blocking and thermal stability at elevated temperatures with a proven magnitude of strength improvement.

directions.direction: Minor microalloying (Co addition) to enhance solid solution and precipitate formation
directions.assessment: Adding a small amount of an element with a smaller atomic radius (e.g., Co) can increase lattice distortion and facilitate the nucleation of beneficial phases. Prior evidence (PMC8074761) supports its role in solid solution strengthening and precipitation. The intervention is precise and testable.

candidates.hypothesis: A controlled post-deposition annealing treatment of a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy containing 5 at.% Al will induce the in situ formation of coherent γ′ precipitates, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature yield strength by approximately 20% relative to the as-cast alloy.
candidates.intervention: Subject the as-cast alloy to a two-step heat treatment: first, a solution treatment at ~1100 °C for homogenization, then aging at ~750–800 °C for 2–4 hours to promote the nucleation and growth of coherent γ′ precipitates.

candidates.hypothesis: Implementing a direct energy deposition (DED) process with a rapid cooling rate (≥10^4 K/s) followed by a short annealing step just below the recrystallization temperature will produce an ultra-fine grained Ti–Ni primary HEA, resulting in a 15–25% increase in elevated-temperature yield strength relative to conventionally cooled alloys.

candidates.hypothesis: Addition of 3 vol.% Y2O3 during spark plasma sintering of a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy will lead to the in situ formation of entropy-stabilized nano-dispersoids that enhance elevated-temperature strength by 40–80% compared to a dispersion-free alloy.
candidates.intervention: Introduce 3 vol.% Y2O3 nanoparticles into the alloy powder prior to spark plasma sintering to trigger formation of nano-dispersoids during consolidation.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of 2 at.% Co into a Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy will enhance lattice distortion and facilitate the formation of a beneficial secondary phase, resulting in an approximate 10–15% improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the Co-free alloy.
